correctness.rationale: For all real payoff advantages greater than one, the sample-two response is twice the current share minus its square. When the high-sample best response requires at most two successes, the transformed drift has constant \(2\alpha-1\) and strictly positive subsequent coefficients, proving that any interior fixed point is repelling. When at least three successes are needed, a binomial union bound at explicit \(\varepsilon\) and \(\alpha\) creates a positive-negative-positive drift sign profile and hence an attracting interior state. The threshold condition is exactly \(k>2(u+1)\), including all tie boundaries. A standard-library exact checker performed 227 direct rational and integer coefficient, threshold and witness checks; the symbolic proof establishes arbitrary k and u.

originality.rationale: The initiating article characterizes when heterogeneous sample sizes can produce stable miscoordination in broad terms but uses sufficiently large higher sample sizes; it does not identify the exact finite cutoff in the two-and-k family for arbitrary payoff advantage. Theorems 1 and 2, their explanatory examples, and Appendix A.6 were compared by logical implication. A narrower low-payoff five-observation boundary is a special case, but does not determine the unbounded all-payoff staircase or any higher transition. An exact binomial-odds coefficient obstruction and an explicit rational construction yield the new full boundary. Targeted mathematical-record and web searches found no covering statement; an unindexed equivalent is not ruled out.

value.rationale: The paper’s qualitative stability-by-heterogeneity observation makes the information cost of stable miscoordination a natural unknown invariant. The theorem determines the least admissible larger sample size for every payoff advantage, with infinitely many sharp integer steps, a tie-driven transition law, a uniform all-degree obstruction, and an explicit rational sufficient mixture. It is structurally stronger than an isolated finite numerical cutoff and relevant to optimal observation budgets.
